parent.name: Blackmar-Diemer Gambit
parent.overview: White offers a pawn with 1.d4 d5 2.e4 dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.f3, aiming for rapid development, the open f-file and a kingside attack with Bc4, Nge2 or Bf4, castling, g4/h4 and Qe1-h4 ideas against h7. Black accepts with 4...exf3 5.Nxf3 and can choose among the Euwe (5...e6), Ziegler (5...c6), Teichmann (5...Bg4) and Bogoljubov (5...g6) defences, or decline with the Lemberger Countergambit 3...e5. With accurate defence Black consolidates the pawn, trades pieces and heads for a better endgame; engines and master opinion call White's compensation insufficient, which is why it is almost never seen at top level. Below master level it scores very well because the attack is easy to play and hard to defend against. The game is typically open and tactical.

root.name: Three Knights Opening: Winawer Defense
root.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Nc3 f5

parent.name: Three Knights Opening
parent.overview: A flexible, classical development move: White puts a second knight on c3 instead of choosing a bishop move. Most games go 3...Nf6, the Four Knights, which has a quiet, somewhat drawish reputation but includes sharp variations (4.Bb5 Spanish, 4.d4 Scotch). Black can avoid that with 3...Bb4, 3...g6 or 3...f5 (the Schliemann-type Gothic/Winawer), or play 3...Bc5 or 3...d6, which White meets with 4.Nxe5 or 4.d4. White's usual plans are d2-d4 to open the centre and Nd5 to dominate it. The 'Three Knights' label in play mostly covers Black's non-Nf6 sidesteps, which are rare among masters.

parent.name: French Defense: Knight Variation
parent.overview: 2.Nf3 is a waiting move that leaves White's central structure undecided. After 2...d5 White can transpose to the Advance (3.e5 c5 4.d4, the subtree's main line), the Exchange (3.exd5 exd5 4.d4), main French lines (3.Nc3) or play for a King's Indian Attack set-up with d3, g3, Bg2 and castling. In the KIA the e5 square is held by pieces (Nf3, Re1) rather than the d4 pawn, which sidesteps the French d4 target. Black's replies are 2...d5 (by far the most common) and the rare 2...f5 (Franco-Hiva Gambit). It is treated in the sources as a secondary option rather than a main-line weapon, and the sources give little independent material on it.

root.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Accelerated Mannheim Variation
root.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 dxc4 3. Qa4+

parent.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted
parent.overview: After 2...dxc4 Black has taken the c-pawn, but sources agree he cannot keep it without serious concessions; White regains it with Bxc4 once the e-pawn has moved (3.e3 or 3.Nf3 then e3, or 3.e4). Black instead gives up the idea of holding it and fights for central counterplay: ...c5 (and ...cxd4) or ...e5 to undermine d4, and ...a6 with ...b5 to gain queenside space and time for the c8 bishop. The centre is open, White has the d4/e4 pawns and the move, and the usual middlegames are IQP or hanging-pawn positions with piece play. Character varies by line: the 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Bxc4 c5 main line is positional and balanced, while 3.e4 lines can be tactical early. It is sound and has been a regular at the elite level since the 1990s.

root.name: Scandinavian Defense: Kloosterboer Gambit
root.moves: 1. e4 d5 2. exd5 c6 3. dxc6 e5

parent.name: Sicilian Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.e4 with ...c5 to trade a flank pawn for White's d-pawn, which leaves Black a central pawn majority and a half-open c-file in return for White's lead in development and space. This asymmetry is the point: Black plays for a win rather than equality. The usual pattern is White attacking on the kingside while Black counterattacks on the queenside along the c-file (...b5, ...Rc8), often with opposite-side castling in the sharpest lines. The root is a crossroads: after 2.Nf3 (about 80% of master games, s1) it branches into Najdorf, Dragon, Scheveningen, Classical, Sveshnikov, Taimanov and Kan, which range from forcing and theory-heavy (Najdorf, Dragon, Sveshnikov) to flexible and solid (Kan, Classical, Taimanov). White's anti-Sicilians (Alapin, Closed, Grand Prix, 2.d3) avoid the Open Sicilian and are quieter. The root as a whole is the most played and most analysed opening at club and master level (s1).

parent.name: Petrov's Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Nxe5 d6 4. Nf3 Nxe4
parent.overview: Black answers 2.Nf3 by counter-attacking e4 rather than defending e5. After 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.d4 d5 6.Bd3 both sides have lost an e-pawn and the structure is symmetrical, with the e-file the main open line. Black's aim is to equalise by quick development and piece trades; White tries to turn a small lead in development or slightly freer play into pressure, often castling and using the e-file or a queenside castling and pawn storm. The 3.d4 Steinitz line (3...Nxe4 4.Bd3 d5 5.Nxe5 Nd7) and 3.Nc3 (Four Knights transposition) or 3.d3 sidelines give quieter or more varied structures. The main lines are widely played at the top and are known as drawish, though some lines hold real attacking chances for both sides.

parent.name: French Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...e6 and ...d5, accepting a pawn chain and a space deficit in return for a sound position, and then hits White's pawn centre at its base with ...c5. The fight is over the dark squares d4 and e5. Black's problem piece is the light-squared bishop on c8, hemmed in by the e6 pawn; Black solves it by exchanging it or rerouting it (...b6 and ...Ba6, or ...Bd7 with ...Bb5/a4). White typically uses extra space for a kingside attack (f4-f5, and in the Advance the g4/h4 ideas) or expands on the queenside with a3-b4. Play is slower and manoeuvring, with a lot of pawn-break play. It has a reputation for solidity but a cramped early game for Black. The Winawer (3.Nc3 Bb4) is the sharpest branch, the Advance is the main fight in a locked centre, and the Tarrasch, Classical and Exchange are quieter. The root is one position after 1...e6 2.d4 d5; the structures differ strongly by branch.

parent.name: Modern Defense
parent.overview: Black plays 1...g6 and 2...Bg7 and lets White build the e4-d4 centre, delaying ...Nf6 (which separates it from the Pirc), then attacks the centre with ...c5, ...e5 or ...Nc6 and the pressure of the g7 bishop. It is a simple, repeatable set-up that Black can adopt against almost anything, and its flexible move order makes it a practical surprise weapon. White's main tries are the Standard line (2.d4 Bg7 3.Nc3 d6 4.f4 or 3.Nf3), the Averbakh-style 2.c4 / 2.Nc3 set-ups, and c3 to blunt the g7 bishop; White often attacks on the kingside with f4, while Black seeks counterplay against an over-extended centre. Sources call it sound but with a risk of passivity or of letting White build an overwhelming centre; it is moderately popular (about 1.7% of games in 2025 on one database) with occasional master use (Suttles, Davies, McNab, Carlsen).
